“So bad it’s good” is, in many ways, a genre unto itself. Film largely dominates, best exemplified by the likes of Plan 9 from Outer Space and Troll 2, but there have been TV series like Riverdale or Baywatch, the latter of which is being rebooted on Fox in 2027. Every once in a while, even the most well-respected series have an episode or two that fall into the category. Buffy the Vampire Slayer, for one, had Season 4's "Beer Bad," where an enchanted beer turns characters into cavemen. What Is 'Star Trek: The Next Generation's "Sub Rosa" About?

In Season 7's "Sub Rosa," the USS Enterprise orbits Caldos IV, where a Scottish-themed colony is established, in order for Dr. Beverly Crusher (Gates McFadden) to attend the funeral of her grandmother, Felisa (Ellen Albertini Dow). She returns to the Enterprise with several mementos from Felisa's home, including some diaries where she discovers her 100-year-old grandmother had relations with a 34-year-old man, Ronin (Duncan Regehr). Beverly returns to her grandmother's home, where she's confronted by the groundskeeper, Ned (Shay Duffin), who warns her never to light Felisa's candle, as doing so will awaken a ghost.

That ghost is Ronin, who takes form and tells Beverly that he loves her, as he has all the women in her family. Ronin continues to manipulate Beverly's mind, eventually coercing her into lighting the candle and abandoning her post on the Enterprise to stay on Caldos IV with him. Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) reluctantly agrees to let her go, but shortly after visits Beverly at her home, wanting to get to know Ronin. Ronin, however, doesn't like the line of questions Picard is asking and attacks, leaving as she tends to her unconscious captain.

blocks.x: Meanwhile, an energy source that is wreaking havoc with the colony's weather modification is found by Data (Brent Spiner) and Geordi LaForge (Levar Burton) . . . in Felisa's grave. They exhume the body, which comes to life and zaps them both. Felisa isn't actually alive, though, but rather is possessed by Ronin. By now, Beverly has figured out the truth: Ronin is an anaphasic alien whose survival hinges on the plasma-based candle that is his energy receptacle. Just as Ronin goes to possess her, Beverly destroys the candle with her phaser, vaporizing Ronin.

blocks.x: "Sub Rosa" is a greatest hits package of what makes a project "so bad it's good." There's the Scottish groundskeeper played by an Irishman whose accent and fervent speech are hilarious. The scene where Felisa rises from the dead brings to mind Tor Johnson's spotty resurrection in the aforementioned Ed Wood classic. Beverly talking with Troi (Marina Sirtis) about her Big O and how she finds her grandmother's diaries erotic (the perfectly-timed shudder from Picard is the cherry on top). The whole side story about the weather inadvertently creates an ironic situation where the colony wants to mirror Scotland, just not its weather patterns.

The one element that this Season 7 episode shares with its "so bad it's good" kin is earnestness, which prevents such fare from being simply bad, and everyone involved with "Sub Rosa" is all in. Yes, it's campy and largely eschews the series' sci-fi leanings in favor of a Gothic horror love story (the psycho-babble about the whole anaphasic alien thing is one of a few attempts to bridge the two), but it's fun, which is exactly what McFadden herself has come to realize:

“When I saw the ‘Sub Rosa’ script, I was like, ‘You are kidding me.’ Patrick hated it. He was like ‘This is absurd’ and all. And when you read it, there are so many completely absurd things in it. And it’s more like a little Gothic, I don’t know horror or something, but yeah, now I embrace it because I think it is hilarious. I mean, I just, I’ve learned to love the green-eyed orgasm that Crusher has, you know? I mean, that doesn’t happen every day, a green-eyed orgasm…”

In defense of "Sub Rosa," there are scenes that are legitimately spooky, particularly before Ronin reveals himself, with Felisa's old home well-suited for creating that haunting atmosphere. Up until its final moments, the episode gets full marks for embracing the supernatural aspect, much of which falls on an excellent performance from McFadden, who sells the fears and joys that overcome Beverly throughout. The most spooky thing about it all? The thought that Beverly's 100-year-old granny was getting some sweet ghost lovin' from a seemingly 34-year-old man. Cue the Picard shudder.
